---
title: "Pre-calculated effects"
subtitle: "When the paper already gives the effect and you only need to pool"
---

Use this module when you extracted the already calculated effect from the
papers, rather than the raw counts. That is the typical case for hazard ratios
(HR) from survival analyses, which rarely come with enough data to recompute.

Follow [the three-step flow](flow.qmd). Here I cover the three input formats and
the field that decides whether your analysis comes out right.

## Step 1, the data

There are three submodules, chosen on the previous page. Pick the one that
matches what you managed to extract from the papers.

| Format | Required columns | Needs a standard error? |
|---|---|:---:|
| TE with 95% CI | `study`, `TE`, `lower`, `upper` | no |
| TE with standard error | `study`, `TE`, `seTE` | yes |
| Full set | `study`, `TE`, `seTE`, `lower`, `upper` | yes |

`n.e` and `n.c` are optional in all three formats and appear in the forest plot
when present. Any other column stays available for subgroup analysis and
meta-regression.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What each format asks for
**TE with 95% CI** is the only one where you type no standard error at all: the
app derives it from the interval. The other two ask for `seTE` directly.
:::

The **Data check** verifies the columns, counts the studies and validates the
interval, requiring `lower <= TE <= upper`. If you swapped two columns, it warns
you here, before the analysis runs.

## Step 2, the parameters

### Outcome settings

**Outcome name**, **If the outcome increases, is that beneficial or harmful?**,
**Experimental group name** and **Control group name** work as in the binary
module.

**Summary measure (sm)** (default `HR`) offers six options, and here it does
more than label the axis: it decides whether your numbers go through a log
transformation.

* Ratio measures: `HR`, `RR`, `OR`. Pooling happens on the log scale and the
  result returns to the original scale in the plots.
* Difference measures: `RD`, `MD`, `SMD`. No transformation.

### The scale of TE

This is where mistakes happen most, and it is worth reading carefully.

For ratio measures, MetaVidence expects the value **as reported in the paper**,
not the logarithm. If the paper says "HR 0.76 (95% CI 0.61 to 0.95)", you type
0.76, 0.61 and 0.95. Typing the logarithm makes the app reject the spreadsheet,
since it requires positive values for ratio measures.

For difference measures, the value is already on the right scale and nothing is
transformed.

::: {.callout-important}
## Check sm before running
The `sm` chosen in **Outcome settings** decides whether your numbers go through
the log transformation. Choosing `MD` when the data are ratios, or the other way
round, produces a result that looks plausible and is wrong. It is the kind of
error no validation catches, because every number is valid.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Careful: `seTE` goes on a different scale from `TE`
For ratio measures the two fields do not share a scale. `TE` goes in as
reported, 0.76. `seTE` goes in on the **log scale**, which is how papers report
it and how the calculation uses it. For the example above, `seTE` would be
0.113, not 0.087.

Getting this wrong raises no error at all: you get a plausible confidence
interval that is wrong. The way to avoid the decision altogether is the **TE
with 95% CI** format, which needs no `seTE`.
:::

### Statistical settings (advanced)

**Analysis model**, **Tau method**, **Random CI method** and **Prediction
method** work exactly as in
[the flow](flow.qmd#statistical-settings-advanced).

**Prediction interval** is off by default (`No`) in all three submodules.

There is no **Method** field: the effect already comes calculated, so pooling is
always by inverse variance.

## Step 3, export and results

Every card from the binary module is here, with the same behavior: **Forest
plot**, **Leave-one-out analysis**, **Funnel plot**, **Small-study effects**
with Egger's test, **Subgroup analysis** and **Meta-regression**, plus the two
summary tables as XLSX.
